power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.formatted: Studies that examine stigma towards mental illness have commonly used explicit measures (i.e. clinical vignettes, self-report scales and experimental paradigms), with over 400 measures reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">18]</ref>.

text.text: Explicit measures assess for stigmatising reactions that are assumed to be consciously controllable, reflective and readily available to recall or report [19].
text.formatted: Explicit measures assess for stigmatising reactions that are assumed to be consciously controllable, reflective and readily available to recall or report <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Despite their ease of implementation and strong face validity [20], explicit tools have been criticised for underplaying the stigma endorsed by mental health clinicians [1].
text.formatted: Despite their ease of implementation and strong face validity [20], explicit tools have been criticised for underplaying the stigma endorsed by mental health clinicians <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, some explicit measures have shown weak correlations with behavioural discrimination [21], and numerous researchers contend that explicit measures may be contaminated by external influences, such as social desirability and professional context [22].
text.formatted: Indeed, some explicit measures have shown weak correlations with behavioural discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[21]</ref>, and numerous researchers contend that explicit measures may be contaminated by external influences, such as social desirability and professional context <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Social desirability presents a real methodological and ethical concern as clinicians may be motivated to underreport or distort stigmatising beliefs given their role [23].
text.formatted: Social desirability presents a real methodological and ethical concern as clinicians may be motivated to underreport or distort stigmatising beliefs given their role <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[23]</ref>.

text.text: This could be to maintain a positive self-image as a carer or to be viewed more favourably by others.

text.formatted: Hence, attempts have been made by researchers to use alternative measures of stigma, with the aim of circumventing the limitations of explicit measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Implicit measures of stigma are assumed to assess reactions that are automatic, spontaneous, and possibly outside of conscious awareness, knowledge and control [25].

text.text: Implicit tools aim to uncover subtle associations held by clinicians between certain concepts (e.g., a psychiatric diagnosis) and attributes (e.g., strange, gloomy etc.) that may lead to negative evaluations [28].

Nevertheless, implicit stigma has been found to predict clinical outcomes.

text.text: Lastly, there is limited appraisal of the methodological quality and risk of publication bias for studies exploring the implicitexplicit correlations of stigma.
Hence, a systematic synthesis and evaluation of the association between these measures of stigma among clinicians is warranted.

The current review aims to address gaps in research by systematically searching and statistically pooling the correlations of implicit and explicit stigma of mental illness by mental health clinicians using a meta-analysis.
This review also aims to examine if any moderators influence the relationship between implicit and explicit stigma, given the correlations may be inconsistent across studies.

Further, the review will synthesise sample and study characteristics, their methodological quality, their risk of publication bias, and consider how implicit and explicit stigma measures relate to clinical outcomes.
Lastly, the review will discuss the main implications of its findings for future research and practice.

However, only 10 studies were included in the systematic review, highlighting a dearth of research on the relation between implicit and explicit stigma among mental health clinicians.
Although some spread of countries was found, no studies were conducted among low-to-middle income countries.

This could limit the generalizability of findings for countries with different sociocultural and political contexts, which may influence the formation and degree of stigma endorsed by clinicians [93].

text.text: There was some variation in the diagnosis of mental illness explored across studies, which included schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and substance use disorders.

However, no studies examined common mental health problems including anxiety or depression, or highly stigmatised psychiatric labels such as personality or dissociative disorders, emphasising a gap for future research [94].
text.formatted: However, no studies examined common mental health problems including anxiety or depression, or highly stigmatised psychiatric labels such as personality or dissociative disorders, emphasising a gap for future research <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[94]</ref>.

text.text: Most studies also did not address the component of stigma being examined through implicit and explicit measures, or how these relate to one another, which aligns with findings from other reviews [7].
text.formatted: Most studies also did not address the component of stigma being examined through implicit and explicit measures, or how these relate to one another, which aligns with findings from other reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Response rates were only reported in four studies but were generally low, meaning samples may have introduced response bias.
Most studies also recruited mixed samples of clinicians, but the correlational data was frequently not available for sub-groups.
This meant we were unable to assess whether type of mental health clinician or training stage moderated the implicit-explicit relationship, which may be interesting to explore in future research.
Demographic reporting was also inconsistent across studies, although from the available data, samples were largely white and female, which may limit generalizability of findings.
Most implicit measures were variants of the implicit-association paradigm.

Despite this, there was considerable variation in the number of implicit tests utilised, along with different target stimuli, concept words and attribute words depending on the mental illness explored.

Some studies provided a comparison category, while other studies did not, meaning that implicit stigma measures were might weaken the interpretability of implicit stigma endorsement across studies and their relation to explicit measures.
These measures also varied considerably, ranging from established questionnaires to ad-hoc scales.
Although two explicit scales were designed to correspond directly with the implicit measures, most did not correspond directly and relied on self-report, which remains subject to social desirability.
These methods may partly account for the low correlations between implicit and explicit stigma across studies.
The weak correlation between implicit and explicit stigma suggests that self-reported attitudes toward PMI among clinicians do not necessarily correspond with automatic or lesscontrolled beliefs.
However, the clinical implications of these findings are challenging to interpret given the correlational design of studies.

It could mean that clinicians endorse neutral or even positive beliefs about PMI when asked by self-report, but in reality demonstrate some implicit stigma, questioning the validity of explicit measures (i.e., through under-estimating stigma) [24].
text.formatted: It could mean that clinicians endorse neutral or even positive beliefs about PMI when asked by self-report, but in reality demonstrate some implicit stigma, questioning the validity of explicit measures (i.e., through under-estimating stigma) <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, it could indicate that explicit stigma among clinicians is accompanied by neutral or positive implicit beliefs, or that different components of stigma are being reflected in the implicit and explicit tools administered.

However, research remains unclear what processes the implicit measures actually capture, thereby questioning the validity of implicit measures (i.e., rather than assuming they capture automatic and unconscious attitudes) [22].
text.formatted: However, research remains unclear what processes the implicit measures actually capture, thereby questioning the validity of implicit measures (i.e., rather than assuming they capture automatic and unconscious attitudes) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Determining whether implicit and explicit stigma predict different clinical outcomes is also challenging, as studies exploring this question were not systematically synthesised in the current review.
This means that conclusions about the outcomes of stigma cannot be drawn from our 10 outcomes were extracted and have been provided in Table 5.
text.formatted: This means that conclusions about the outcomes of stigma cannot be drawn from our 10 outcomes were extracted and have been provided in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: Findings suggest that implicit and explicit stigma may contribute to different clinical behaviours (e.g., helping intentions) and jobrelated outcomes (e.g., intention to change jobs) for clinicians which aligns with previous research [34].
text.formatted: Findings suggest that implicit and explicit stigma may contribute to different clinical behaviours (e.g., helping intentions) and jobrelated outcomes (e.g., intention to change jobs) for clinicians which aligns with previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[34]</ref>.

text.text: Findings on the association between exposure to PMI and implicit or explicit stigma were inconsistent.
Future reviews should examine the outcomes of implicit and explicit stigma among mental health clinicians using the appropriate search strategy to synthesise all available studies.
There may also be ethical implications arising from these findings.

If implicit and explicit beliefs are only weakly related, this raises questions about transparency and self-awareness in clinical practice, particularly for clinicians who, through training and reflective work, recognise their own implicit biases yet explicitly endorse socially desirable beliefs (such as providing impartial care for PMI) [28].

text.text: This dissonance may also be uncomfortable for clinicians [95], as inconsistent implicit and explicit beliefs can predict increased stress and absenteeism from work [71].

text.text: Addressing these discrepancies is important for safeguarding equitable healthcare and for supporting the wellbeing of clinicians.
Findings indicate the need for stigma-reduction efforts that consider both implicit and explicit dimensions of stigma [21].
text.formatted: Findings indicate the need for stigma-reduction efforts that consider both implicit and explicit dimensions of stigma <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[21]</ref>.

text.text: However, it is acknowledged that stigma-reduction initiatives normally address explicit stigma only among mental health clinicians, through educational campaigns that may not always be sufficient to reduce implicit stigma [96].
text.formatted: However, it is acknowledged that stigma-reduction initiatives normally address explicit stigma only among mental health clinicians, through educational campaigns that may not always be sufficient to reduce implicit stigma <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[96]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, providing interventions that promoted continuum-beliefs and recovery-oriented perspectives reduced explicit stigma towards voice hearing and depression across clinician samples, but produced no change in their implicit scores [49, 58, 97].
text.formatted: Indeed, providing interventions that promoted continuum-beliefs and recovery-oriented perspectives reduced explicit stigma towards voice hearing and depression across clinician samples, but produced no change in their implicit scores <ref type="bibr">[49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">97]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, interventions must not assume that changing self-reported beliefs will translate into shifts in implicit beliefs, as these may be more automatic, stable, and resistant to psychoeducation [25].
text.formatted: Consequently, interventions must not assume that changing self-reported beliefs will translate into shifts in implicit beliefs, as these may be more automatic, stable, and resistant to psychoeducation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[25]</ref>.

text.text: This systematic review provides the first comprehensive pooling of correlations between implicit and explicit stigma among mental health clinicians.
In doing so, it directly addresses a gap highlighted in previous reviews and responds to recommendations [30, 47].
text.formatted: In doing so, it directly addresses a gap highlighted in previous reviews and responds to recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">47]</ref>.

text.text: Strengths include a comprehensive search strategy, critical quality appraisal, high agreement rates between reviewers, and moderator analyses.
The review also incorporated sensitivity analyses, tests of publication bias, and prediction intervals to ensure robustness of findings.
Importantly, it examined studies across several clinical settings, professions and countries, all of which employed varying aims, designs, and measures of stigma, thereby broadening its scope.

Finally, by linking the pooled correlations to dualprocess theories and identifying substance use disorder as a key moderator, this review provides both theoretical and clinical contributions that extend beyond previous reviews.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
Most included studies were cross-sectional and only baseline correlations were extracted.
This precludes conclusions about the causal relationship and temporal stability of associations between implicit and explicit stigma.

Longitudinal and experimental designs are needed to clarify if changes in one attitude system influences the other over time, along with how these systems map onto clinical decision making and outcomes for PMI.
As grey literature was not included, and only English-language publications were reviewed, it is possible that relevant studies were missed through our search strategy.
Studies exploring neuropsychiatric conditions (e.g., neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders) were also not extracted.
This narrows the scope of our findings, despite the frequent co-occurrence of mental health symptoms in these populations [98, 99].
text.formatted: This narrows the scope of our findings, despite the frequent co-occurrence of mental health symptoms in these populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">[98,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">99]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, as this review explored group level findings, it does not capture variability among implicit and explicit associations for individual clinicians.
There are several avenues for future research.
First, it is important for primary research to replicate the main findings among larger-scale studies with a more diverse sample of clinicians and countries to support generalisability.

Second, studies may benefit from clarifying the dimensions of stigma being investigated among implicit and explicit measures, which in turn may improve our theoretical understanding, and target stigma-reduction efforts.
Third, studies could explore how implicit and explicit stigma actually shape clinical outcomes for PMI in longitudinal studies.
This may clarify if implicit and explicit evaluations map onto distinct causal pathways to predict different intentions and / or behaviours exhibited by mental health clinicians.
These might include automatic and spontaneous behaviours, or deliberative and controlled behaviours towards PMI [45].
text.formatted: These might include automatic and spontaneous behaviours, or deliberative and controlled behaviours towards PMI <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[45]</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, primary research might be enhanced from approaches such as single-case experimental designs, to track individual changes in implicit and explicit stigma from mental health clinicians over time.

Future reviews could assess the social desirability, spontaneity, psychometric properties and correspondence of implicit and explicit measures across studies, along with the effort required to retrieve implicit and explicit cognitions among clinicians [36].
text.formatted: Future reviews could assess the social desirability, spontaneity, psychometric properties and correspondence of implicit and explicit measures across studies, along with the effort required to retrieve implicit and explicit cognitions among clinicians <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[36]</ref>.

text.text: These variables might impact the correlations reported.

Future reviews may also wish to explore the relationship between implicit and explicit stigma for neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions, or among undergraduate students in health professions (i.e., medical students), as these were excluded in our review.

It might also be valuable to investigate the relationship among students training in mental healthcare (i.e., trainee psychologists or student mental health nurses), as this could help clarify the influence of clinical training on implicit and explicit stigma, and identify opportunities for early stigma reduction.
This review systematically synthesised evidence from 10 studies examining the relationship between implicit and explicit stigma of mental illness among mental health clinicians.

The pooled correlation was small but statistically significant (r = .13) in line with prior meta-analyses, indicating that implicit and explicit stigma might be related but largely distinct constructs.
